Content:
In this lesson, we will continue our exploration of surface areas and volumes of similar solids.

Content:
Consider the similar rectangular prisms shown below:

Graphic:

Content:
Prism [MATH: E] (on the left) has a side length of [MATH: 7\,\text{cm}], while prism [MATH: F] (on the right) has a side length of [MATH: 21\,\text{cm}]. Suppose we are told that the surface area of prism [MATH: F] is [MATH: 567\,\text{cm}^2] and its volume is [MATH: 1701\,\text{cm}^3]. Using this information, we want to determine the surface area and volume of prism [MATH: E].

Content:
Recall from a previous lesson that if the lengths of a three-dimensional object are enlarged by a scale factor of [MATH: k] then the surface area of the new shape will be enlarged by a scale factor of [MATH: k^2] and the volume of the new shape will be enlarged by a scale factor of [MATH: k^3].

Content:
Here, the smaller prism is similar to the larger one with a scale factor of
[MATH: k = \dfrac{7\,\textrm{cm}}{21\,\textrm{cm}} = \dfrac{1}{3}.]

Content:
Thus, the ratio of the surface areas is [MATH: k^2 = \left(\dfrac13\right)^2 = \dfrac19,] and we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\mathcal{A}_E}{\mathcal{A}_F} = \dfrac{1}{9}.]

Content:
Solving for [MATH: \mathcal{A}_E] and substituting in [MATH: \mathcal{A}_F = 567\,\textrm{m}^2,] we get
[MATH: A_{E}|= (1)/(9) ⋅ A_{F}; = (1)/(9) ⋅ 567cm^{2}; = 63cm^{2}.]

Content:
For volumes, the ratio is given by the cube of the scale factor:

Content:
[MATH: k^3 = \left(\dfrac13\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{27}.]

Content:
So we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{V_E}{V_F} = \dfrac{1}{27}.]

Content:
Solving for [MATH: V_E] and substituting in [MATH: V_F = 1701\,\textrm{cm}^3,] we get
[MATH: V_{E}|= (1)/(27) ⋅ V_{F}; = (1)/(27) ⋅ 1701cm^{3}; = 63cm^{3}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If two solids are similar with scale factor [MATH: k,] then the ratio of the corresponding volumes equals [MATH: k^3.]

Here, the larger cone ([MATH: Q]) is similar to the smaller one ([MATH: P]) with a scale factor of [MATH: k = \dfrac{9\,\textrm{in}}{6\,\textrm{in}} = \dfrac{3}{2}.]

Thus, the ratio of the volume is [MATH: k^3 = \left(\dfrac32\right)^3 = \dfrac{27}{8},] and we have [MATH: \dfrac{\mathcal{V}_Q}{\mathcal{V}_P} = \dfrac{27}{8}.]

Solving for [MATH: \mathcal{V}_Q] and substituting [MATH: \mathcal{V}_P = 56\,\textrm{in}^3,] we get [MATH: V_{Q}|= (27)/(8) ⋅ V_{P}; = (27)/(8) ⋅ 56; = 189in^{3}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If two solids are similar with scale factor [MATH: k,] then the ratio of the corresponding surface areas equals [MATH: k^2.]

Since prism [MATH: Q] has a surface area that is [MATH: 36] times that of prism [MATH: P,] we have [MATH: \dfrac{\mathcal{A}_Q}{\mathcal{A}_P} = 36.]

This means that the prisms are similar with a scale factor of [MATH: k = \sqrt{36} = 6.]

Thus, the ratio of the heights is [MATH: \dfrac{h_Q}{h_P} = 6.]

Solving for [MATH: h_Q] and substituting in [MATH: h_P = 10\,\textrm{cm},] we get [MATH: h_{Q}|= 6 ⋅ h_{P}; = 6 ⋅ 10cm; = 60cm.]

sections.normalized_html: Two triangular prisms, [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q,] are similar. The surface area of prism [MATH: P] is [MATH: 36\,\textrm{in}^2,] and the surface area of prism [MATH: Q] is [MATH: 324\,\textrm{in}^2.] If the volume of prism [MATH: P] is [MATH: 50\,\textrm{in}^3,] what is the volume of prism [MATH: Q?]
sections.readable_text: Two triangular prisms, [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q,] are similar. The surface area of prism [MATH: P] is [MATH: 36\,\textrm{in}^2,] and the surface area of prism [MATH: Q] is [MATH: 324\,\textrm{in}^2.] If the volume of prism [MATH: P] is [MATH: 50\,\textrm{in}^3,] what is the volume of prism [MATH: Q?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If two solids are similar with scale factor [MATH: k,] then

  • the ratio of the corresponding surface areas equals [MATH: k^2,] and

  • the ratio of the corresponding volumes equals [MATH: k^3.]

Here, prism [MATH: Q] is larger than prism [MATH: P.] Computing the ratio of the surface areas, we have [MATH: \dfrac{\mathcal{A}_Q}{\mathcal{A}_P} = \dfrac{324\,\textrm{in}^2}{36\,\textrm{in}^2} = 9.]

This means that the solids are similar with a scale factor of [MATH: k = \sqrt{9} = 3.]

Thus, the ratio of the volumes is [MATH: k^3 = 3^3 = 27,] and we have [MATH: \dfrac{\mathcal{V}_Q}{\mathcal{V}_P} = 27.]

Solving for [MATH: \mathcal{V}_Q] and substituting in [MATH: \mathcal{V}_P = 50\,\textrm{in}^3,] we get [MATH: V_{Q}|= 27 ⋅ V_{P}; = 27 ⋅ 50in^{3}; = 1,350in^{3}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we will continue our exploration of surface areas and volumes of similar solids.

Content:
Consider the similar rectangular prisms shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a0b2c92b7a0c92bc87974178ca8768e0]

Content:
Prism [MATH: E] (on the left) has a side length of [MATH: 7\,\text{cm}], while prism [MATH: F] (on the right) has a side length of [MATH: 21\,\text{cm}]. Suppose we are told that the surface area of prism [MATH: F] is [MATH: 567\,\text{cm}^2] and its volume is [MATH: 1701\,\text{cm}^3]. Using this information, we want to determine the surface area and volume of prism [MATH: E].

Content:
Recall from a previous lesson that if the lengths of a three-dimensional object are enlarged by a scale factor of [MATH: k] then the surface area of the new shape will be enlarged by a scale factor of [MATH: k^2] and the volume of the new shape will be enlarged by a scale factor of [MATH: k^3].

Content:
Here, the smaller prism is similar to the larger one with a scale factor of
[MATH: k = \dfrac{7\,\textrm{cm}}{21\,\textrm{cm}} = \dfrac{1}{3}.]

Content:
Thus, the ratio of the surface areas is [MATH: k^2 = \left(\dfrac13\right)^2 = \dfrac19,] and we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\mathcal{A}_E}{\mathcal{A}_F} = \dfrac{1}{9}.]

Content:
Solving for [MATH: \mathcal{A}_E] and substituting in [MATH: \mathcal{A}_F = 567\,\textrm{m}^2,] we get
[MATH: A_{E}|= (1)/(9) ⋅ A_{F}; = (1)/(9) ⋅ 567cm^{2}; = 63cm^{2}.]

Content:
For volumes, the ratio is given by the cube of the scale factor:

Content:
[MATH: k^3 = \left(\dfrac13\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{27}.]

Content:
So we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{V_E}{V_F} = \dfrac{1}{27}.]

Content:
Solving for [MATH: V_E] and substituting in [MATH: V_F = 1701\,\textrm{cm}^3,] we get
[MATH: V_{E}|= (1)/(27) ⋅ V_{F}; = (1)/(27) ⋅ 1701cm^{3}; = 63cm^{3}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If two solids are similar with scale factor [MATH: k,] then the ratio of the corresponding volumes equals [MATH: k^3.]

Here, the larger cone ([MATH: Q]) is similar to the smaller one ([MATH: P]) with a scale factor of
[MATH: k = \dfrac{9\,\textrm{in}}{6\,\textrm{in}} = \dfrac{3}{2}.]

Thus, the ratio of the volume is [MATH: k^3 = \left(\dfrac32\right)^3 = \dfrac{27}{8},] and we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\mathcal{V}_Q}{\mathcal{V}_P} = \dfrac{27}{8}.]

Solving for [MATH: \mathcal{V}_Q] and substituting [MATH: \mathcal{V}_P = 56\,\textrm{in}^3,] we get
[MATH: V_{Q}|= (27)/(8) ⋅ V_{P}; = (27)/(8) ⋅ 56; = 189in^{3}.]
